about.title: San Marcos Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Falls rarely announce themselves. One moment you are walking into a store off W San Marcos Boulevard or crossing a parking lot near S Rancho Santa Fe Road, and the next you are on the ground with a wrist that will not bend the right way. In California, the property owner is not automatically at fault for that. What matters is notice: whether the owner or the business knew about the wet floor, the broken step, or the uneven pavement, or reasonably should have known and did nothing to fix or warn about it. That is the piece that decides most San Marcos premises cases, and it is why the days right after a fall are so important. Photos of the hazard, the names of anyone who saw it, and a prompt request that the property preserve its surveillance footage can make the difference between a claim that holds together and one that fades. LawProactive is a free service, not a law firm. We connect San Diego County residents with an independent attorney who reviews the facts and, if the case is taken, works on contingency.

whyChoose.title: Why San Marcos Residents Reach Out to LawProactive

items.title: Attorneys who understand the notice rule
items.desc: California requires proof that the owner knew or should have known about the hazard. The attorneys in our network know how to look for cleaning logs, prior complaints, and inspection records that speak to that question.

items.title: Deadlines tracked from day one
items.desc: Most premises claims carry a two-year filing window, but a fall on city or other public property in San Marcos triggers a much shorter deadline. Getting connected early keeps those dates from slipping past.

items.title: Fair treatment under comparative fault
items.desc: California uses pure comparative fault, so a claim is not lost even if you were partly to blame; it is reduced by your share. An attorney can push back when a property owner tries to shift more of that share onto you than the facts support.

items.question: I fell on a sidewalk in San Marcos. Is the city responsible?
items.answer: It depends on who owns and maintains that stretch of sidewalk and whether the defect was one the responsible party knew or should have known about. If a public entity such as the City of San Marcos or San Diego County is involved, the deadline to act is considerably shorter than the two years that applies to private property. Because of that, it is worth having an attorney sort out ownership quickly rather than waiting to see how your injuries heal.

items.question: The store says there was a wet floor sign. Does that end my claim?
items.answer: Not necessarily. A sign is one factor, but questions remain about where it was placed, whether it was visible from your approach, and whether the hazard should have been cleaned up rather than simply marked. Under California's pure comparative fault rule, even if you are assigned some responsibility, your claim is reduced rather than eliminated.

items.question: How do I get the surveillance video from the business where I fell?
items.answer: Many businesses record over footage within days or weeks, so timing is critical. An attorney can send a written preservation request right away, which puts the property on notice not to delete the recording. In the meantime, take your own photos of the hazard and note the exact time and location so the footage can be pinpointed.
